defenses.limitations: Removable media, laptops, supply-chain compromise and unofficial bridges can cross the gap. Claimed isolation must be verified.
defenses.example: A sensitive control system exchanges approved files only through a controlled transfer procedure.

defenses.definition: Network boundary enforcement designed for assessed industrial control environments.
defenses.mechanism: Restrict allowed communication and, where supported, inspect relevant industrial protocol operations.
defenses.conditions: Useful between engineering, supervisory and process zones when rules are developed with operations and safety staff.
defenses.limitations: An unsafe rule can disrupt physical processes. Firewalls do not replace controller hardening, recovery or independent safety systems.
defenses.example: A plant boundary allows only approved engineering paths and rejects unnecessary controller access.

defenses.definition: Dividing a network into security zones with controlled communication between them.
defenses.mechanism: Define allowed paths and enforce them through suitable routing, firewall or equivalent policy.
defenses.conditions: Useful for limiting lateral movement and reducing blast radius across workloads or device fleets.
defenses.limitations: An unconstrained VLAN is not sufficient isolation. Permitted vulnerable services and shared management paths can bridge zones.
defenses.example: An IoT camera zone cannot initiate connections to employee workstations.

defenses.definition: Enforcement devices or host controls that permit or block traffic according to configured policy.
defenses.mechanism: Restrict unnecessary services and crossings between network security boundaries.
defenses.conditions: Useful for reducing reachable paths and limiting propagation through unwanted services.
defenses.limitations: Allowed flows may carry attacks; policy errors and encrypted visibility limits remain. A firewall does not patch a vulnerable host.
defenses.example: A host firewall blocks an unused service that a worm otherwise could reach.

defenses.definition: Controls that inspect activity and can block traffic matching supported attack conditions.
defenses.mechanism: Apply signatures or behavioral rules inline at an assessed enforcement point.
defenses.conditions: Useful against known exploit patterns with appropriate tuning and sufficient visibility.
defenses.limitations: False positives can interrupt service, and evasion or encrypted traffic can hide attacks. It does not replace patching.
defenses.example: An IPS rejects a recognized exploit request targeting an unpatched service while remediation is arranged.

defenses.definition: A Linux mandatory access-control system enforcing policy beyond ordinary discretionary permissions.
defenses.mechanism: Labels and policy rules constrain which resources and operations a process may use.
defenses.conditions: Useful for limiting container and host process access when enforcing mode and appropriate policy are maintained.
defenses.limitations: Permissive mode, overly broad policy and kernel vulnerabilities can undermine confinement. It does not make privileged containers universally safe.
defenses.example: A container process is denied access to host files outside its approved SELinux policy.

defenses.definition: Operating-system mechanisms providing separated views of processes, mounts, networks or other resources.
defenses.mechanism: Assign workloads to appropriately configured namespaces to reduce unintentional sharing and visibility.
defenses.conditions: Useful as one component of container isolation on a supported patched host.
defenses.limitations: Namespaces do not alone provide a complete security boundary; capabilities, mounts, host sockets and kernel vulnerabilities matter.
defenses.example: A container has its own process and mount views while separate policy restricts privileged operations.

defenses.display_name: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)
defenses.definition: Email-domain policy and reporting based on aligned SPF or DKIM results.
defenses.mechanism: A domain publishes policy and receivers assess alignment with the visible From domain under DMARC rules.
defenses.conditions: Useful against some unauthorized use of a protected domain in email, with carefully deployed enforcement.
defenses.limitations: It does not certify message content, stop look-alike domains or prevent abuse of a compromised legitimate account.
defenses.example: A company progresses to an enforced DMARC policy after reviewing legitimate mail flows and reports.

defenses.definition: Procedures that constrain how payments and account-detail changes are approved.
defenses.mechanism: Use independent verification, separation of duties, transaction limits and reconciled records.
defenses.conditions: Useful when deceptive communications attempt to turn a valid business workflow into fraud.
defenses.limitations: Collusion, weak exception paths and compromised approvers can undermine the process. Approval does not replace account security.
defenses.example: A changed payee requires confirmation through a known supplier contact and a second authorized approver.

defenses.definition: Training adapted to high-value roles, authority pressure and sensitive business decisions.
defenses.mechanism: Practice delegation, payment verification and secure handling of board or acquisition material with relevant staff.
defenses.conditions: Useful for executives and assistants targeted by tailored deception.
defenses.limitations: Role-specific training does not override the need for technical controls or independent transaction checks.
defenses.example: An executive assistant practices challenging an urgent request that claims normal approvals must be skipped.

defenses.definition: Documented steps for confirming a sensitive request through evidence independent of its delivery channel.
defenses.mechanism: Use established contact information, dual approval or separately authenticated records before accepting changed instructions.
defenses.conditions: Useful for transfers, credential recovery and privileged access changes.
defenses.limitations: A second channel controlled by the same attacker is not independent. Procedures need exceptions that cannot silently bypass verification.
defenses.example: Finance confirms altered supplier bank details using the supplier's pre-existing verified contact record.

defenses.definition: Limiting access to valuable data according to verified business needs.
defenses.mechanism: Apply resource-specific permissions, review grants and log sensitive retrieval or export.
defenses.conditions: Useful for reducing the reach of a compromised or deceived executive or other user.
defenses.limitations: It does not establish whether a communication is genuine or stop misuse of legitimately accessible data.
defenses.example: A transaction team limits acquisition documents to approved participants instead of a broad executive group.

defenses.definition: Restricting which services accept or initiate network connections through firewall policy.
defenses.mechanism: Close unused listening services and apply assessed ingress and egress rules.
defenses.conditions: Useful for reducing unnecessary access paths to remote-control services.
defenses.limitations: A Trojan may use an allowed outbound connection or trusted service; port blocking alone is not malware cleanup.
defenses.example: A workstation policy denies unneeded inbound remote-control ports and monitors unexpected outbound sessions.

defenses.definition: Identifying observations that differ from a defined expected pattern.
defenses.mechanism: Compare activity with an assessed baseline or model and send meaningful deviations for investigation.
defenses.conditions: Useful for unusual destinations, process chains or identity activity when context is available.
defenses.limitations: An unusual event is not necessarily malicious, and attackers can imitate normal behavior. Baselines require maintenance.
defenses.example: A workstation contacting a new external control endpoint at unusual hours triggers review.

defenses.definition: Separating a suspected compromised system from sensitive resources while preserving appropriate response access.
defenses.mechanism: Restrict network paths, invalidate sessions where needed and use trusted systems for recovery decisions.
defenses.conditions: Useful for containing malware and avoiding sensitive work in a compromised browser or endpoint.
defenses.limitations: Isolation is not eradication; it can disrupt business and must preserve safety and evidence needs.
defenses.example: A suspected infected laptop is isolated from production access while responders collect evidence.

defenses.definition: Redirecting selected malicious infrastructure traffic to a controlled defensive destination.
defenses.mechanism: Use appropriate legal and technical authority to alter resolution or routing for a known command endpoint.
defenses.conditions: Useful for disrupting some botnet control channels and identifying affected clients.
defenses.limitations: Alternative command paths and embedded addresses can bypass it. Sinkholing does not remove malware and must not capture unrelated traffic.
defenses.example: A coordinated defender operation redirects a botnet domain to a monitored defensive server.

defenses.definition: Reducing or eliminating an assessed Windows NTLM authentication path.
defenses.mechanism: Inventory dependencies, audit usage and enforce appropriate restrictions while migrating required services.
defenses.conditions: Useful against NTLM-specific credential reuse when supported alternatives and compatibility have been verified.
defenses.limitations: It can break legacy services and does not stop Kerberos ticket/key abuse or all credential theft. Some paths may remain unless explicitly covered.
defenses.example: An organization retires NTLM for a tested service and verifies that fallback is no longer accepted.

defenses.definition: A ticket-based network authentication protocol using a trusted key distribution service.
defenses.mechanism: Clients obtain and present service tickets according to domain identity and trust policy.
defenses.conditions: Useful in appropriately managed environments as part of reducing legacy authentication exposure.
defenses.limitations: Kerberos is not a universal pass-the-hash remedy; stolen keys or tickets, weak delegation and NTLM fallback remain risks.
defenses.example: A service accepts properly validated Kerberos tickets after its authentication dependencies are reviewed.

defenses.definition: Authorization in which permissions are assigned to roles and identities receive approved role memberships.
defenses.mechanism: Enforce the role's permitted operations at resource boundaries and review membership lifecycle.
defenses.conditions: Useful for managing consistent job-based access in applications and cluster APIs.
defenses.limitations: Overbroad roles, inherited rights and compromised members can still cause harm. RBAC does not enforce every workload security setting.
defenses.example: A cluster user can inspect workloads but cannot create privileged administrative resources.

defenses.definition: Rules that assess workload security settings before resources are accepted into a cluster.
defenses.mechanism: Use supported controls such as Pod Security Admission and appropriate admission policy to restrict privileged workloads and unsafe host access.
defenses.conditions: Useful for new or changed workloads together with API authorization and runtime protection.
defenses.limitations: The removed PodSecurityPolicy API should not be deployed as a current feature. Admission policy does not fix every running workload or kernel flaw.
defenses.example: A cluster rejects a manifest requesting prohibited host privileges under its enforced workload standard.

defenses.definition: Maintaining components through verified supported releases that correct known defects.
defenses.mechanism: Inventory versions, assess applicability, test where needed and verify deployment of the required update.
defenses.conditions: Useful when a known security flaw has a supported fix.
defenses.limitations: An update is not proof that a previously compromised device is clean; unsupported products may require replacement.
defenses.example: A camera fleet receives a tested vendor release addressing a remotely exploitable service flaw.

defenses.definition: Checking a sender's identity and request using appropriate technical evidence and trusted channels.
defenses.mechanism: Inspect authenticated domain signals and confirm sensitive requests independently when risk warrants it.
defenses.conditions: Useful for targeted messages that exploit familiarity or current business details.
defenses.limitations: A compromised legitimate mailbox can pass domain checks. Authentic sender identity does not prove benign intent.
defenses.example: An engineer confirms a sensitive document request with the known project lead through an established channel.

defenses.definition: A broad category of controls that identify or block malicious content and activity.
defenses.mechanism: Specify the actual product capability, telemetry, prevention policy and response process rather than relying on the label.
defenses.conditions: Useful when a concrete threat path and supported detection or blocking function are identified.
defenses.limitations: The term is not a standardized guarantee. Unknown attacks, missing visibility and configuration gaps can defeat coverage.
defenses.example: A mail-and-endpoint deployment links a malicious attachment alert to containment of the affected workstation.

defenses.definition: Controlled practice of security decisions and response procedures.
defenses.mechanism: Use authorized scenarios with defined learning goals, safe execution and constructive feedback.
defenses.conditions: Useful for rehearsing phishing reporting, verification and incident escalation before a real event.
defenses.limitations: A simulation does not authenticate a real request or prove future immunity. Exercises must not harm operations or shame individuals.
defenses.example: A team rehearses independent verification of a tailored supplier-payment request.

defenses.definition: Rules controlling access to web destinations or selected web content.
defenses.mechanism: Block known harmful sites or categories through an assessed proxy, resolver or endpoint enforcement point.
defenses.conditions: Useful for restricting access to a known compromised site while incident response proceeds.
defenses.limitations: New destinations, encrypted visibility limits and policy bypasses can reduce coverage. A permitted site can still be malicious.
defenses.example: A known watering-hole site is temporarily blocked for managed browsers during investigation.

defenses.definition: Collection and analysis of endpoint activity with investigation and response capabilities.
defenses.mechanism: Correlate process, file, identity and network behavior and support actions such as containment.
defenses.conditions: Useful for investigating activity that signatures alone may miss when telemetry and staff coverage are sufficient.
defenses.limitations: Blind spots, tampering and alert overload remain possible. An installed agent is not evidence that every attack is prevented.
defenses.example: A browser exploit leads to unusual process behavior, prompting endpoint isolation and forensic review.

defenses.definition: Inspection of files, systems or configurations for specified threats or weaknesses.
defenses.mechanism: Use an appropriate vulnerability, malware or configuration scanner and verify findings in context.
defenses.conditions: Useful for identifying known problems before deployment or during investigation.
defenses.limitations: Scanning scope and signatures limit coverage; unknown behavior and unsafe device classes may be missed. A clean result is not proof of safety.
defenses.example: A removable file is scanned in a controlled environment before an approved transfer.

defenses.definition: Execution policy permitting only approved applications or code identities.
defenses.mechanism: Rules based on assessed publishers, hashes or other supported attributes limit what can run.
defenses.conditions: Useful on managed systems with controlled software needs and a maintained approval process.
defenses.limitations: Approved interpreters and signed vulnerable tools can be abused. Overbroad publisher rules or weak administration reduce protection.
defenses.example: A managed workstation refuses an unapproved fake support utility despite a user's attempt to run it.

defenses.definition: Detection based on suspicious actions and relationships rather than only known file identifiers.
defenses.mechanism: Observe relevant behavior such as unusual persistence, injection or credential access and investigate correlations.
defenses.conditions: Useful for malware variants and abuse of legitimate tools where sufficient telemetry exists.
defenses.limitations: Heuristics can be bypassed or mistaken, and detections need operational response.
defenses.example: A signed tool's unusual chain of actions triggers investigation despite its apparently legitimate file signature.

defenses.definition: Detection and remediation of recognized malicious files and related execution behavior.
defenses.mechanism: Use updated signatures and other supported detection techniques with quarantine and investigation.
defenses.conditions: Useful as an endpoint layer against file-infecting malware and other supported threats.
defenses.limitations: Novel or concealed malware may evade detection, and removal may not restore trust after privileged compromise.
defenses.example: A file-infecting malware signature triggers quarantine and checks of other executable files.

defenses.definition: Practices and browser protections that reduce exposure to deceptive or malicious web content.
defenses.mechanism: Use trusted navigation, supported browsers and cautious handling of downloads and unexpected prompts.
defenses.conditions: Useful for everyday risk reduction in combination with endpoint and identity controls.
defenses.limitations: A familiar site can be compromised and careful users can still encounter browser exploits.
defenses.example: A user retrieves an application from a verified publisher route rather than an advertisement impersonating it.

defenses.definition: Filtering attack traffic in sufficiently provisioned infrastructure before forwarding acceptable traffic to the protected service.
defenses.mechanism: Route traffic through a mitigation service that distinguishes assessed attack patterns from legitimate demand.
defenses.conditions: Useful when local link capacity would otherwise be exhausted before on-premises controls can act.
defenses.limitations: Application-layer floods, routing setup and false positives require planning; no service has unlimited capacity.
defenses.example: A provider diverts a volumetric flood away from the customer's constrained access circuit.

defenses.definition: Examining flow, packet and application observations to understand behavior and anomalies.
defenses.mechanism: Measure rates, sources, destinations and protocol behavior and correlate them with service symptoms.
defenses.conditions: Useful for diagnosing DoS/DDoS and informing appropriate filtering or escalation.
defenses.limitations: Analysis alone does not absorb or block a flood. Collection visibility and privacy constraints limit conclusions.
defenses.example: Operations staff distinguish a traffic surge from a distributed attack before activating mitigation.

defenses.definition: Working with a connectivity provider on upstream visibility and mitigation.
defenses.mechanism: Use established incident contacts to arrange routing, filtering or scrubbing before a constrained customer link.
defenses.conditions: Useful for attacks whose volume or source cannot be handled at the local edge.
defenses.limitations: Response capability, lead time and collateral effects vary by agreement and provider. It is not automatic attack prevention.
defenses.example: An organization activates its provider's agreed DDoS escalation procedure during a sustained flood.

defenses.definition: A protocol protecting a network session's confidentiality and integrity with peer authentication as configured.
defenses.mechanism: Negotiate supported cryptography and verify the intended certificate identity and trust chain.
defenses.conditions: Useful against interception on a protected path when endpoints and trust configuration are reliable.
defenses.limitations: It does not protect data after a malicious browser decrypts it or prove that a look-alike site's operator is benign.
defenses.example: A client rejects an intermediary's certificate because it is not valid for the intended server identity.

defenses.definition: Restricting a client to an expected certificate or public-key identity beyond ordinary trust-store acceptance.
defenses.mechanism: A managed application checks an approved pin set during its protected connection process.
defenses.conditions: Useful in narrowly controlled clients with a robust update, recovery and key-rollover design.
defenses.limitations: Bad rollover can cause outages; pinning is not generally suitable for arbitrary browser sites and does not cure endpoint compromise.
defenses.example: A controlled device client accepts only the planned service key set and its carefully staged successor.

defenses.definition: An authenticated encrypted tunnel carrying selected traffic between specified trusted endpoints across another network.
defenses.mechanism: Encapsulate traffic across an untrusted segment after verifying the tunnel peer and enforcing routing policy.
defenses.conditions: Useful for protecting traffic between the client and trusted tunnel endpoint.
defenses.limitations: It does not authenticate every visited site, make a hostile Wi-Fi login safe or protect data after tunnel termination.
defenses.example: A remote employee forms a verified organizational tunnel before accessing internal services.

defenses.definition: Randomizing memory placement to make exploitation that relies on predictable addresses harder.
defenses.mechanism: The platform varies locations of code, libraries, stacks or other mapped regions according to its implementation.
defenses.conditions: Useful as a memory-exploitation mitigation with adequate entropy and compatible binaries.
defenses.limitations: Information leaks, limited entropy and code-reuse techniques can weaken it. It does not remove an out-of-bounds memory bug.
defenses.example: A process uses randomized library placement while developers repair a vulnerable parser.

defenses.definition: Guard values placed around certain stack data to detect selected overwrite patterns.
defenses.mechanism: Compiler-generated checks detect unexpected guard changes before a protected function returns.
defenses.conditions: Useful as one layer against some stack-based buffer-overflow techniques.
defenses.limitations: Not every object or overwrite is covered, and a leaked guard may be bypassed. They do not establish memory safety.
defenses.example: A protected program aborts after an oversized input corrupts a stack guard.

defenses.definition: Browser add-ons providing defined capabilities under explicit permission and update controls.
defenses.mechanism: Allow only justified extensions from assessed sources and monitor permissions and changes.
defenses.conditions: Useful for specific supported browser protections where the extension's authority is appropriate.
defenses.limitations: Extensions can themselves steal data or alter transactions. Adding an arbitrary extension is not a reliable defense against a compromised browser.
defenses.example: An administrator removes an unapproved extension with broad access to banking pages and investigates the endpoint.

defenses.definition: A family of controls protecting different parts of name resolution and DNS administration.
defenses.mechanism: Specify whether the objective is DNSSEC validation, protected resolver transport, registrar security or resilient authoritative service.
defenses.conditions: Useful only when the chosen mechanism is tied to the actual DNS threat path.
defenses.limitations: Encrypted DNS does not authenticate unsigned zone data, and DNSSEC does not encrypt queries or prevent every registrar-account takeover.
defenses.example: A design separates signed-data validation from encrypted client-to-resolver transport rather than calling both one generic fix.

defenses.definition: Inspection of message attributes and content to reduce delivery of harmful mail.
defenses.mechanism: Evaluate attachments, URLs, sender signals and malicious patterns with quarantine and reporting workflows.
defenses.conditions: Useful at mail gateways and endpoints when rules and detection data are maintained.
defenses.limitations: Novel lures and compromised senders can pass checks; false positives require review. Delivery is not a trust certification.
defenses.example: A gateway quarantines a recognized malicious attachment before it reaches an employee mailbox.

defenses.definition: Role-appropriate instruction for recognizing unsafe requests and following verified workflows.
defenses.mechanism: Teach concrete actions and reporting paths using relevant examples and reinforcement.
defenses.conditions: Useful as a human layer alongside usable technical and organizational controls.
defenses.limitations: Training does not guarantee recognition or excuse unsafe system design. Outcomes should not depend on perfect vigilance.
defenses.example: Staff practice checking a document-sharing request through the known service rather than an unexpected link.

defenses.display_name: Independent navigation instead of unexpected text links
defenses.definition: A user practice of reaching services through known applications or addresses rather than unverified SMS destinations.
defenses.mechanism: Discard the untrusted destination and verify the claim through an established entry point.
defenses.conditions: Useful for reducing exposure to account, payment and delivery lures in texts.
defenses.limitations: A known application or device can still be compromised, and some legitimate services use texts. The practice is not a guarantee.
defenses.example: A customer opens the bank's known app rather than following an alarming text-message link.

defenses.definition: Device protections that detect or restrict harmful mobile applications, destinations or configurations.
defenses.mechanism: Use supported platform capabilities, management policies and appropriate threat detection.
defenses.conditions: Useful for managed devices with supported operating systems and a defined response process.
defenses.limitations: Sandboxing limits what a scanner can observe; social deception and new threats may remain. Tool claims need capability verification.
defenses.example: A managed phone warns about an unapproved risky application and reports its installation to administrators.

defenses.definition: Classification or blocking of suspicious text messages by device, carrier or service policy.
defenses.mechanism: Use sender, content and abuse signals to identify likely unwanted or malicious messages.
defenses.conditions: Useful as one layer against mass text lures and known malicious patterns.
defenses.limitations: Spoofed sender information, novel wording and legitimate-looking threads can evade filtering; false positives are possible.
defenses.example: A device moves a known fraudulent delivery text into its spam folder.

defenses.display_name: Certificate authority trust and identity validation
defenses.definition: A trust service and validation process binding public keys to asserted identities under a defined policy.
defenses.mechanism: Clients verify certificate chains, intended names, validity and application-specific identity requirements.
defenses.conditions: Useful for authenticating enterprise Wi-Fi servers and other TLS peers when client trust is configured correctly.
defenses.limitations: A certificate from any CA is not sufficient for any identity. Misissued certificates, unsafe user overrides and compromised endpoints remain risks.
defenses.example: A Wi-Fi client rejects an authentication-server certificate not valid for its configured organization server.

defenses.definition: Finding wireless devices or configurations inconsistent with authorized infrastructure.
defenses.mechanism: Combine sensor observations, inventory and network evidence to locate and investigate suspected rogue access points.
defenses.conditions: Useful for organizational wireless assessment and incident response.
defenses.limitations: Similar names do not prove malice, and detection does not guarantee prevention before a user connects.
defenses.example: An alert identifies an access point imitating a managed network name and prompts physical investigation.

defenses.definition: Client policy preventing untrusted or obsolete network profiles from being joined automatically.
defenses.mechanism: Remove unnecessary remembered networks and require appropriately authenticated network configurations.
defenses.conditions: Useful against deceptive responders exploiting automatic association behavior.
defenses.limitations: A user can still select a malicious network manually; a remembered name alone never proves network identity.
defenses.example: A managed laptop no longer probes for and automatically joins an old public guest network.

defenses.definition: Representing untrusted output so the receiving format treats it as data, not executable syntax.
defenses.mechanism: Choose the encoder for the exact HTML, attribute or other supported output context and use safe rendering APIs.
defenses.conditions: Useful when displaying plain untrusted text inside a known safe context.
defenses.limitations: Encoding for one interpreter is not safe for another; some script or URL contexts should not accept interpolation at all.
defenses.example: An application encodes a comment before displaying it as plain HTML text.

defenses.definition: A browser-enforced policy restricting resource loading and script execution for a page.
defenses.mechanism: Use carefully designed directives, nonces or hashes and avoid unnecessary unsafe execution allowances.
defenses.conditions: Useful as defense in depth against some script injection and unexpected resource loading.
defenses.limitations: It does not replace safe output handling; permissive policy or trusted-script abuse can undermine it.
defenses.example: A site permits only expected scripts with appropriate nonce handling while fixing the underlying injection defect.

defenses.definition: Parsing and restricting intentionally permitted rich content to a defined safe subset.
defenses.mechanism: Use a maintained sanitizer suitable for the browser context instead of ad hoc string removal.
defenses.conditions: Useful when an application deliberately allows limited formatting or markup.
defenses.limitations: Parser differences, unsafe configuration and later mutation can reintroduce script execution. Sanitization is not needed in place of simple text encoding.
defenses.example: A comment editor retains basic formatting but removes active content through a maintained HTML sanitizer.

defenses.definition: Resolving path representations and verifying that access remains within an authorized resource scope.
defenses.mechanism: Handle encodings, separators and platform rules, then use safe file APIs and a verified allowed root.
defenses.conditions: Useful when applications accept resource paths rather than opaque identifiers.
defenses.limitations: Naive string-prefix checks, symbolic links and check/use races can bypass confinement even after normalization.
defenses.example: A download service rejects a resolved file path that escapes its authorized export directory.

defenses.definition: Changing a process's apparent filesystem root on supported Unix-like systems.
defenses.mechanism: Limit normal path resolution to a designated tree with appropriate permissions and privilege reduction.
defenses.conditions: Useful as a containment layer in carefully configured services.
defenses.limitations: Chroot is not a complete sandbox; privileged processes and unsafe open descriptors may escape intended restrictions.
defenses.example: A minimally privileged service receives a restricted filesystem view alongside other isolation controls.

defenses.definition: Protection for specified robust Wi-Fi management frames when supported and negotiated.
defenses.mechanism: Authenticate relevant management traffic to reduce forgery such as certain deauthentication messages.
defenses.conditions: Useful when infrastructure and clients enforce the required protected-management configuration.
defenses.limitations: Not all management frames are covered and radio jamming remains possible. Compatibility and transition settings need verification.
defenses.example: A modern wireless deployment requires protected management frames for compatible clients.

defenses.definition: Sensors that identify suspicious activity and raise alerts rather than inherently blocking it.
defenses.mechanism: Inspect network or host telemetry using supported signatures, protocol checks or analytics.
defenses.conditions: Useful when sensor placement, visibility and incident response make alerts actionable.
defenses.limitations: Detection gaps and false positives remain; encrypted payloads may be unavailable. An IDS is not automatically an IPS.
defenses.example: A wireless sensor alerts on a burst of suspicious disconnect messages for investigation.

defenses.definition: Logical separation of local network traffic into defined broadcast domains.
defenses.mechanism: Assign interfaces and apply appropriate inter-VLAN routing and access policy at controlled boundaries.
defenses.conditions: Useful for organizing and separating traffic when enforcement and switching configuration are correct.
defenses.limitations: A VLAN is not encryption or complete authorization. Misconfiguration and permitted routing can expose traffic across segments.
defenses.example: A guest device VLAN cannot directly reach an administrative segment because routing rules enforce that separation.

defenses.definition: Establishing that a claimant corresponds to an asserted real-world or organizational identity.
defenses.mechanism: Evaluate appropriate evidence and independent checks using a process proportionate to the risk.
defenses.conditions: Useful for enrollment, account recovery and issuing replacement credentials when identity must be re-established.
defenses.limitations: Proofing differs from authenticating a returning user and from authorizing a particular action. Public trivia is weak evidence.
defenses.example: An account-recovery team verifies the employee through approved evidence before issuing a replacement authenticator.

defenses.definition: Training tied to the decisions and responsibilities people actually have.
defenses.mechanism: Use realistic tasks, clear verification steps and reinforcement that fits operational workflows.
defenses.conditions: Useful for impersonation and misleading-information risks alongside enforceable controls.
defenses.limitations: A course completion record does not prove correct action under pressure or remove a technical weakness.
defenses.example: Reception staff practice a safe response to someone claiming a senior employee's identity.

defenses.definition: Policy limiting which USB devices or device classes may be used.
defenses.mechanism: Block unapproved storage or other supported classes through operating-system and endpoint controls.
defenses.conditions: Useful against untrusted removable media when legitimate peripheral needs are assessed.
defenses.limitations: Storage-only rules may not block a device emulating a keyboard or network adapter. Physical access remains a separate concern.
defenses.example: A managed workstation refuses an unapproved removable storage device found in a hallway.

defenses.definition: Organizational rules specifying approved behavior, responsibilities and exceptions.
defenses.mechanism: Translate policy into workable procedures and technical enforcement where possible, then monitor adherence.
defenses.conditions: Useful for removable media, data handling and requests involving trust.
defenses.limitations: A written rule alone cannot stop a device or authenticate a caller. Unsafe exception practices can defeat the rule.
defenses.example: A media-transfer policy requires approved devices and a controlled inspection route.

defenses.definition: Physical entry spaces designed to control passage through sequential doors.
defenses.mechanism: Interlocks and authorization checks can limit entry to an assessed number of people at a time.
defenses.conditions: Useful for restricted facilities with appropriate supervision, safe egress and accessibility design.
defenses.limitations: Piggybacking detection and emergency behavior depend on the design; unsafe confinement is unacceptable.
defenses.example: A laboratory entry vestibule checks individual authorization before opening the interior door.

defenses.definition: Systems that associate a presented credential with access permissions at a physical boundary.
defenses.mechanism: Readers and controllers enforce door rights and retain relevant entry records.
defenses.conditions: Useful for managed facility access with prompt revocation and secure credential technology.
defenses.limitations: Shared or cloned badges, tailgating and weak recovery procedures can bypass identity assumptions.
defenses.example: A departed employee's badge rights are revoked across managed office entrances.

defenses.definition: Trained people who monitor facilities, verify access and respond to security events.
defenses.mechanism: Apply approved challenge, escort and response procedures with situational judgment.
defenses.conditions: Useful where human oversight complements barriers and electronic systems.
defenses.limitations: Staffing, fatigue, deception and unsafe confrontation risks limit coverage. Guards do not substitute for every technical barrier.
defenses.example: A guard verifies a visitor's sponsor through a known internal contact before entry.

defenses.definition: Watching for registrations or changes resembling protected domains and identities.
defenses.mechanism: Compare domain observations with known names and investigate suspicious use before issuing warnings or takedowns.
defenses.conditions: Useful for early discovery of typosquatting and brand impersonation.
defenses.limitations: Similarity is not proof of maliciousness, and monitoring does not block access before a response.
defenses.example: An alert identifies a newly registered one-letter variation of an organization's login domain.

defenses.definition: User-facing alerts when a destination resembles a known site or contains suspicious spelling.
defenses.mechanism: A browser or security layer compares destination patterns and prompts the user to verify before proceeding.
defenses.conditions: Useful as a navigation aid alongside trusted bookmarks and domain verification.
defenses.limitations: Heuristics can miss deceptive names or warn on legitimate ones; users may ignore prompts.
defenses.example: A browser highlights a near-match domain and offers a route to the previously used genuine site.

defenses.definition: A keyed integrity and authenticity construction based on a cryptographic hash.
defenses.mechanism: Parties sharing a secret compute and verify a MAC over the intended message and context.
defenses.conditions: Useful when shared-key authentication fits the protocol and keys are protected.
defenses.limitations: It does not encrypt data, provide public signature verification or automatically supply replay protection. It is not a generic collision repair for every protocol.
defenses.example: A service verifies a request MAC and separately checks the message's freshness.

defenses.definition: Selecting reviewed cryptographic primitives that provide the properties required by a protocol.
defenses.mechanism: Replace deprecated constructions through a tested design with suitable security strength and implementation support.
defenses.conditions: Useful when old collision-sensitive or otherwise broken primitives remain in use.
defenses.limitations: An algorithm name alone does not make a protocol secure; modes, trust, keys and implementation details still matter.
defenses.example: A signing workflow migrates from a collision-broken hash to a supported reviewed construction.

defenses.definition: Physical barriers designed to resist specified forced-entry conditions.
defenses.mechanism: Strengthen the door, frame, hinges, anchoring and locking assembly together.
defenses.conditions: Useful for delaying forced access as part of a risk-assessed facility design.
defenses.limitations: A strong panel with a weak frame can fail. Fire egress, accessibility and alternate routes remain important.
defenses.example: A facility upgrades a vulnerable service entrance with a rated integrated assembly.

defenses.definition: Sensors and notification systems that detect selected access or tamper events.
defenses.mechanism: Door, motion or other detectors trigger monitored alerts with defined response responsibility.
defenses.conditions: Useful for recognizing and responding to attempted or completed forced entry.
defenses.limitations: An alarm does not physically stop entry, and false alarms or delayed response can limit benefit.
defenses.example: A forced-open door event reaches a staffed response function with the correct location.

defenses.definition: A Wi-Fi configuration that omits the SSID from some routine broadcast advertisements.
defenses.mechanism: The network may be absent from a simple visible list, while other management exchanges still reveal identifying information.
defenses.conditions: At most an administrative presentation choice, not a meaningful substitute for wireless authentication or encryption.
defenses.limitations: It does not make radio activity or the SSID secret, and probing behavior can create privacy issues. Do not teach it as a wardriving defense.
defenses.example: A wireless survey still identifies a network whose access point suppresses normal SSID advertising.

defenses.definition: Assessing a claim against original evidence and credible independent corroboration.
defenses.mechanism: Check dates, context, source provenance and what the evidence actually supports; retain uncertainty where appropriate.
defenses.conditions: Useful for suspected misinformation, hoaxes and exaggerated incident claims.
defenses.limitations: Sources can be wrong or incomplete; popularity and repeated reporting may trace to one unreliable origin.
defenses.example: An analyst finds that an alleged current breach image actually documents a much older unrelated outage.

defenses.definition: Policy-based review and handling of material on a managed platform.
defenses.mechanism: Apply stated standards through proportionate review, restriction, removal and appeal workflows.
defenses.conditions: Useful for reducing exposure to harmful or misleading content within a platform's authority.
defenses.limitations: Moderation is not an automatic truth detector and can be inconsistent or overbroad. Legal and contextual considerations matter.
defenses.example: A forum flags an unsupported security warning for review instead of automatically presenting it as verified guidance.

defenses.definition: A standardized symmetric block cipher used within suitable cryptographic constructions.
defenses.mechanism: A secret key transforms fixed-size blocks; an appropriate mode defines how messages are encrypted and authenticated.
defenses.conditions: Useful when the algorithm, mode, nonce handling and key lifecycle fit the application.
defenses.limitations: AES alone is not authenticated encryption, password storage or a complete protocol. Bad mode or key use can defeat the system.
defenses.example: An application uses a reviewed AES-based authenticated mode rather than a proprietary cipher.

defenses.definition: Controls for generating, protecting, distributing, using, revoking and retiring keys.
defenses.mechanism: Separate access, use suitable randomness and storage, track key versions and plan compromise response.
defenses.conditions: Useful throughout encrypted and signed system lifecycles, including planned migration and verified compromise response.
defenses.limitations: Protecting keys does not repair a broken algorithm or unsafe protocol. Losing keys may also make legitimate data unrecoverable.
defenses.example: A service rotates a compromised encryption key and tracks which data requires re-encryption.

defenses.definition: Using appropriate established cryptographic constructions instead of unassessed proprietary inventions.
defenses.mechanism: Match required properties to current standards and validated implementation practice, then test the complete protocol.
defenses.conditions: Useful when selecting or replacing an encryption or authentication design.
defenses.limitations: Compliance with a label does not prove correct configuration, safe randomness or suitability for every use.
defenses.example: A team rejects a custom substitution cipher and adopts an interoperable reviewed protocol design.

defenses.definition: Replacing a secret under a defined lifecycle or compromise condition.
defenses.mechanism: Reissue keys or credentials, revoke old use and update dependents through an authenticated process.
defenses.conditions: Useful after exposure, cryptoperiod limits or algorithm migration where the system design requires it.
defenses.limitations: Routine password changes without evidence are not universally helpful. Rotation does not fix a weak algorithm or malware stealing the replacement.
defenses.example: A leaked service key is revoked and replaced while affected consumers are updated safely.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Hypervisor patching, minimized virtual devices and restricted management reduce known guest-escape attack paths.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Hardening cannot prove the absence of unknown host or firmware vulnerabilities.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Protected integrity baselines can reveal altered boot or system components associated with a rootkit.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A compromised kernel can deceive in-guest tools; baseline and measurement trust must be independent where needed.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Verified boot-chain policy can reject unauthorized startup components and reduce some bootkit persistence.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Signed vulnerable components, compromised firmware and post-boot rootkits remain possible.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Process memory inspection can find injected or memory-resident code not represented by a malicious executable file.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Visibility and rapid execution limit coverage; fileless activity can still leave other artifacts.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Behavior analytics can identify suspicious use of interpreters and legitimate utilities in a fileless execution chain.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Legitimate automation can look unusual; alerts need context and response rather than automatic certainty.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Interpret source verification here as source-network IP anti-spoofing to reject forged reflection requests.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Checking an email sender does not stop reflection; victim-side filtering alone cannot control other originating networks.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Time-limited codes narrow the useful lifetime of captured authentication values when the verifier enforces appropriate checks.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Codes can be relayed or reused inside a window without single-use enforcement; they do not protect arbitrary messages.

mapping_reviews.applicability: An authenticated fresh challenge or one-time nonce can bind a credential proof to its intended exchange.
mapping_reviews.limitations: The receiver must verify freshness or non-reuse; simply including randomness is insufficient.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Configuration and access audits can discover public permissions and verify their remediation.
mapping_reviews.limitations: An audit does not itself remove an exposed bucket policy and can miss changes between checks.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Encryption protects some storage or transport exposure under appropriate key and access arrangements.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not fix anonymous authorized reads when the service decrypts objects for public users; remove public permissions instead.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Removing WEP and deploying a supported modern Wi-Fi configuration eliminates reliance on WEP's broken design.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Client compatibility, configuration and implementation security still need assessment; jamming is unaffected.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Use a cost-tuned salted password KDF to increase the work required per offline password guess.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A fast general-purpose hash, even a modern one, is not adequate password storage merely because it is called strong.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Anti-spyware detection and remediation can identify and remove supported surveillance software.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Novel or privileged surveillance may evade detection, and prior data theft cannot be undone by removal.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Restricting application permissions can reduce accessible sensors and personal data before a low-privilege spyware program collects them.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Privileged malware may bypass settings; permission review does not reliably remove an active infection.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Verified dedicated physical resources can reduce a co-tenant's access to the shared resource causing a leak.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Provider terminology differs; dedicated virtual placement may still share hardware, and same-host leakage can remain.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Proper authenticated encryption rejects modified ciphertext before vulnerable application decryption paths expose padding information.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Correct nonce handling and implementation matter; do not claim that arbitrary encryption with an unrelated checksum suffices.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A controlled change process supports replacement of a cryptographically broken scheme after review and testing.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Change management is not chosen-plaintext security. The mapping needs explicit migration context rather than a prevention claim.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Compatible frequency-agile radios may tolerate some narrow-band interference by using other permitted channels.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Wideband or powerful jamming can affect all channels; this is not universal anti-jamming protection.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Backups may support recovery if a disruption coincides with data loss.
mapping_reviews.limitations: They do not restore radio availability or counter interference; do not teach backups as a jamming defense.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Reduced Bluetooth discovery can lower casual exposure while approved connections remain necessary.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Known device addresses and exploitable services can remain reachable; patching or radio shutdown addresses different risks.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Independent callback verification interrupts reliance on a spoofed caller identity before credentials or authority are released.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A phone number supplied by the suspect caller is not independent verification.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A trusted authenticated support channel can reduce exposure of sensitive information during verified assistance.
mapping_reviews.limitations: An encrypted call can still be fraudulent; transport security alone does not defeat a convincing voice pretext.

mapping_reviews.applicability: An approved challenge-response identity process can test a pretexting requester's claimed identity.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Public biographical questions are weak, and proof of identity does not authorize every requested disclosure.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Enforced handling procedures can define which information staff may disclose to a verified requester.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A privacy notice alone does not authenticate anyone or technically prevent pretexting.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Schema validation rejects malformed authentication messages before protocol processing.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Well-formed forged assertions remain possible without signature, issuer and freshness checks.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Protocol-appropriate identity, signature, audience and freshness checks reject fabricated authentication assertions.
mapping_reviews.limitations: The source attack label is broad; a scenario must name the actual assertion and missing verification.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Monitoring domains, ads and abuse reports can discover impersonating content and support response.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Detection is not authentication of every message and does not automatically remove a fraudulent site.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Education helps users check trusted routes rather than trusting logos or familiar branding.
mapping_reviews.limitations: People cannot reliably identify every impersonation; usable verification and technical controls remain necessary.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Appropriate paper destruction removes readable sensitive records before they enter an uncontrolled waste stream.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Storage media require technology-appropriate sanitization; careless custody can expose records before destruction.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Locked collection containers reduce access before controlled removal and destruction.
mapping_reviews.limitations: They leave the contents recoverable if the lock or collection chain is bypassed.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A screen privacy filter reduces off-axis observation of displayed information.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not stop a camera directly behind the user or observation of keyboard input.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A suitable biometric sign-in can reduce typing of reusable secrets that an observer could record.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not conceal an unlocked screen, prevent screen capture or solve every authentication-recovery path.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Calibrated sensors provide early measurements of heat, water, smoke or power conditions threatening equipment.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Sensors do not repair the condition or determine whether the cause is deliberate.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Independent power, cooling or service paths can preserve operation when an environmental component fails.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Shared failure domains and untested failover can defeat redundancy; backups and redundancy are different controls.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Supported removal tools uninstall unneeded packages and associated services after dependency assessment.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Not all bloatware is malware; privileged compromise may require a more trustworthy recovery process.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A verified clean image can remove accumulated unwanted software when rebuilding is appropriate.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Rebuilding is disruptive and may reinstall the same bundled programs if the image is not corrected.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Appropriate standardized post-quantum public-key mechanisms address identified quantum-vulnerable public-key operations.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Do not imply current quantum computers break every cipher, or that algorithm migration alone secures the whole protocol.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Disabling an unused Bluetooth interface removes that device's unsolicited Bluetooth-message delivery path.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not remove existing malware or protect other wireless interfaces.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Browser ad-request filtering reduces unwanted advertisements and some malvertising exposure.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not uninstall all adware or establish that all permitted content is safe.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Verified distribution sources reduce deceptive or bundled software acquisition.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Legitimate publishers can distribute unwanted software or suffer compromise; reputation is not an integrity guarantee.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Correct context-specific escaping can reduce unsafe shell interpretation in constrained legacy paths.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Prefer avoiding a shell; quoting errors and argument injection can remain even when some metacharacters are escaped.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Explicit allowlists constrain permitted operations and inputs when combined with safe non-shell interfaces.
mapping_reviews.limitations: An approved string can still be interpreted unsafely downstream; verify the complete command construction.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Bound query parameters keep untrusted values from changing SQL syntax.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Dynamic identifiers and unsafe query paths still need controlled selection and review.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A WAF can block recognized SQL injection patterns while code remediation is arranged.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Bypasses and false positives remain; it is not a replacement for separating SQL instructions and data.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Non-executable data pages obstruct injection that depends on executing bytes in those pages.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Code reuse, executable mappings and other injection paths remain; DEP does not remove the vulnerability.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Memory-safe construction and safe process interfaces can remove the defect enabling a specific injection path.
mapping_reviews.limitations: The actual path must be identified; a general secure-coding label cannot certify every process boundary.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Independent source review can identify suspicious destructive triggers before acceptance.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Review may miss obfuscation, dependencies or code introduced after review in the build process.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Restricting changes to sensitive code and scheduled jobs reduces opportunities to plant destructive triggers.
mapping_reviews.limitations: An already authorized maintainer may still abuse permitted access; access controls need separation of duties and oversight.

mapping_reviews.applicability: User behavior analytics can flag unusual access or exports for investigation.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Intent cannot be inferred reliably from anomaly alone; privacy and legitimate role changes require context.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Least privilege limits the resources and actions an insider or stolen account can abuse.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Required legitimate access can still be misused, so this is impact reduction rather than complete prevention.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Appropriate Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite cookie attributes reduce distinct token exposure paths.
mapping_reviews.limitations: No attribute makes a stolen live token universally unusable; XSS and endpoint compromise remain relevant.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Server-enforced idle and absolute lifetime limits reduce the usable window of a stolen session.
mapping_reviews.limitations: An attacker can act before expiration or keep some sessions active; invalidation and reauthentication need additional design.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Authenticated encryption protects data across a path where an intermediary could observe or alter it.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Unauthenticated encryption does not establish peer identity, and compromised endpoints remain outside that guarantee.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Mutual authentication checks both endpoint identities to resist active peer impersonation.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Trust configuration, identity binding and key protection are essential; a protocol label is not proof of correct validation.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Correct DNSSEC validation authenticates signed DNS data against the configured chain of trust.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Unsigned data, registrar compromise and traffic confidentiality are different problems.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Hardened resolvers with appropriate validation and controlled access reduce cache-poisoning exposure.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A resolver's reputation alone does not establish that every response is authenticated.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Switch ARP validation checks advertisements against trusted local address bindings.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Trust-port errors and unhandled static hosts can bypass protection or interrupt service.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Managed fixed ARP bindings prevent unwanted dynamic replacement for selected stable peers.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Manual drift and compromised legitimate devices remain concerns; this does not scale automatically.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Source-network anti-spoofing rejects forged requests before they enlist reflection amplifiers.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Deployment elsewhere is required to stop abuse from other networks; not every DDoS uses spoofed sources.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Relevant boundary rules can close exposed amplifiers or block identifiable abusive service traffic.
mapping_reviews.limitations: The rule must be on an effective path; victim-side filtering cannot restore bandwidth already saturated upstream.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Validate function events and inputs before they influence resource selection or execution.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Valid input can still invoke an overprivileged function, and dependency flaws require additional controls.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Scoped service identities and resource policies reduce the reachable data and actions of a compromised function.
mapping_reviews.limitations: IAM does not repair vulnerable code and overbroad trust relationships can defeat intended boundaries.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A correctly configured modern Wi-Fi deployment removes weaknesses associated with obsolete protocol modes.
mapping_reviews.limitations: WPA3 does not repair every access-point implementation flaw or make transition configurations uniformly safe.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Applicable verified firmware fixes address known wireless implementation vulnerabilities.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Patches must match affected devices, and compromise before patching may require additional response.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Reviewed constant-time sensitive operations reduce certain secret-dependent timing and cache leaks.
mapping_reviews.limitations: The deployed compiler and platform matter; power, fault and other side channels need separate treatment.

mapping_reviews.applicability: An assessed HSM can confine keys and sensitive operations within a hardened boundary.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Not every HSM or operation is free of side channels, and authorized misuse of the key can still occur.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Consistent locking protects a correctly scoped shared-state invariant from unsafe concurrent interleaving.
mapping_reviews.limitations: All participants must use the lock, and deadlocks or cross-process resource changes require design.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A suitable atomic operation or transaction keeps the complete check-and-update invariant indivisible.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Atomic individual reads are insufficient when the security decision spans multiple operations.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Confirmed exposure reports can trigger credential invalidation and investigation before further stuffing attempts.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Breach intelligence is incomplete and delayed; observing exposure does not itself prevent a login.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Different passwords for different services break the cross-service reuse prerequisite of credential stuffing.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A credential stolen from the target service or a compromised password manager remains exposed.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Correlation across accounts and time can identify low-rate password spraying missed by per-account thresholds.
mapping_reviews.limitations: An alert needs response and sufficient telemetry; distributed slow attempts can remain difficult to distinguish.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Appropriate additional authentication factors reduce takeover with a guessed password alone.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Phishable factors, weak recovery and already stolen sessions can undermine protection; prefer phishing-resistant methods.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Removing deprecated versions and weak fallback choices prevents negotiation of those specific options.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Remaining implementations can still have flaws; compatibility and authenticated negotiation need testing.

mapping_reviews.applicability: HSTS reduces browser HTTP fallback for the protected origin after valid policy learning or appropriate preload.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not prevent every TLS protocol downgrade and does not authenticate an unrelated look-alike domain.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Wireless sensors and inventory comparison can find unapproved access points and support assessed response.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Detection can miss radios or misclassify legitimate equipment; automated disruption needs legal and operational review.

mapping_reviews.applicability: MAC lists can assist limited local device administration.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Spoofable MAC addresses do not authenticate an access point or reliably prevent unauthorized AP deployment; do not teach this as rogue-AP prevention.

mapping_reviews.applicability: An on-screen keyboard may bypass a logger that observes only physical key events.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Screen capture, pointer capture and browser hooks can still collect the input; do not present it as endpoint security.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Anti-malware detection can find and quarantine supported software keyloggers.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Hardware loggers and privileged or novel software require different inspection and recovery steps.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Enforced quotas before expensive work reduce request-exhaustion paths within the service's control.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Distributed sources and constrained upstream links can defeat local request-based protection.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Additional independently provisioned service instances can tolerate some workload pressure or instance failures.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Shared dependencies and total capacity remain finite; balancing is not a complete DoS prevention mechanism.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Lockouts or progressive restrictions slow online guesses on the protected authentication path.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Rigid lockouts can be abused for denial of service and do not stop offline cracking or all distributed spraying.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Automation challenges can add friction to some online guessing tools.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Solvers, relays and bypasses exist; CAPTCHA alone is not a sufficient authentication or guessing defense.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Authenticated sequence values and receiver state reject already accepted protocol messages.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Reset, wraparound and session binding must not reopen acceptance of captured values.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A genuinely one-time code can prevent reuse of a particular authentication value when it is bound and checked correctly.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not provide replay protection for arbitrary application commands or prevent live relay before use.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Authenticated fresh challenges or checked one-time nonces prevent acceptance of captured device commands.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Device reset, storage limits and concurrent sessions must not reopen the replay window.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Authenticated timestamps restrict the age of accepted commands with a defined time window.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Repeated messages inside the window remain possible without additional replay tracking; clock rollback must be handled.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Interpret Tokens specifically as server-validated request-bound anti-CSRF values in this mapping.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Generic session or bearer tokens are not automatically anti-CSRF protection; XSS or leaked tokens can defeat it.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Appropriate SameSite policy reduces cookie sending in selected cross-site contexts.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It is not sufficient for every CSRF situation; unsafe endpoints and same-site attacks remain concerns.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Use cryptographic tag authentication with protected keys and fresh challenges, rather than static identifier acceptance.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Encrypted stored data alone does not prevent cloning or relay; reader and protocol design must be assessed.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Appropriate shielding limits opportunities for unauthorized radio reading while the credential is enclosed.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not protect a credential during legitimate use or invalidate a copy already obtained.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Prefer long unique passwords and common-value blocklists over the legacy idea of predictable complexity recipes.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Composition rules alone can produce guessable patterns; phishing and credential theft are different attack paths.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Unique salts prevent shared offline precomputation against stored verifiers.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Salts do not block online dictionary guesses or eliminate offline guessing of an individual weak password.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Per-record random salts make one reusable rainbow-table computation impractical across a user database.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Use an appropriate password KDF too; salts do not create entropy in a weak password.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Cost-tuned password derivation increases the cost of computing candidates or tables.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Cost alone does not diversify records; unique salts are needed to prevent shared precomputation.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Require removal of shared factory defaults during secure provisioning or after confirmed exposure.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Do not reinterpret this as arbitrary periodic password changes without evidence; predictable replacement patterns can remain weak.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Hardening removes unused default accounts and restricts reachable management interfaces.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A baseline must actually check credentials and effective access; generic hardening does not prove every default is gone.

mapping_reviews.applicability: An appropriately chosen SHA-3 variant supplies modern collision resistance for suitable designs.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Output size and intended use matter; it is not a generic password-storage or message-authentication replacement.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Sufficient output size raises generic birthday collision-search cost for an otherwise sound hash construction.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A longer output cannot rescue an algorithm with a practical structural collision weakness.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Independent verification of a support or reward offer checks authority before the requested disclosure or installation.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A vague instruction to verify is insufficient without a trusted evidence route and authorization check.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Practice recognizing exchanges of benefits for secrets can improve refusal and reporting decisions.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Training does not prove the actual requester is legitimate or prevent malware execution by itself.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Physical-access monitoring can reveal unexpected accompaniment or movement after entry.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not necessarily stop an unauthorized visitor at the door; observation needs a safe response process.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Visitor escort procedures limit movement to approved routes and responsible accompaniment.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Compliance, staffing and safe challenge practices determine effectiveness; an unattended visitor can still cross interior boundaries.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A rated installed lock with controlled keys increases resistance to specified manipulation techniques.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Weak frames, alternate entrances and stolen authorized keys can bypass the cylinder.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Electronic access monitoring can detect an unexpected opening or add independent entry verification.
mapping_reviews.limitations: An electronic label does not imply mechanical pick resistance and an alert may occur after entry.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Independent source checking interrupts action based on a fabricated security instruction.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Evidence can be incomplete; verification must include date, applicability and the actual requested action.

mapping_reviews.applicability: An exercised response plan gives staff a safe route to triage questionable incident claims.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A plan alone does not establish that the claim is true or block harmful instructions.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Tested isolated or immutable backups enable data recovery without depending on the extortionist.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Backups do not prevent encryption, undo data theft or guarantee that restored systems are free of persistence.

mapping_reviews.applicability: A specified mail or web gateway can reduce ransomware delivery through its inspected channel.
mapping_reviews.limitations: The broad gateway label is not a universal barrier; direct access, stolen credentials and unknown payloads can bypass it.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Applicable patching removes known exploitation paths used by some ransomware intrusions.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Credential abuse and social engineering can remain, and patching does not reverse existing compromise.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Supplier and build-practice assessments identify risks and enforceable requirements before reliance on a dependency.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A favorable assessment cannot guarantee future publisher or build integrity.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Trusted signature verification detects tampering after signing and binds a release to an accepted publisher key.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A compromised build or signing key can produce a validly signed malicious release; signatures do not prove benign code.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Heuristic or behavior-based detection can identify exploit-like actions before a precise signature exists.
mapping_reviews.limitations: False positives and unseen techniques remain; do not claim that heuristics detect every zero-day.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Assessed intelligence guides hunting and protective priorities as new exploit evidence emerges.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Intelligence can be incomplete or stale and does not itself block an unknown vulnerability.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Strong verified network isolation removes direct remote paths where the operational design permits it.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Media, maintenance laptops and supply-chain routes can cross the boundary; a claimed air gap is not immunity.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Industrial boundary policy restricts approved control-system paths and supported protocol operations.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Unsafe filtering can cause physical-process disruption; safety engineering and operational validation are necessary.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Independent release and publisher verification supports a trustworthy update decision.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A generic verification instruction needs concrete evidence and cannot certify that an authentic publisher was not compromised.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Signature verification with an independently trusted key detects package tampering after signing.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A correctly signed update can still be malicious if the publisher or signing pipeline was compromised.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Enforced zone boundaries limit lateral reach between network segments.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Permitted paths and shared administration can bridge zones; segmentation does not eradicate infected systems.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Service-access rules reduce reachable propagation paths used by a worm.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Allowed vulnerable services and internal paths may still permit spread; firewall policy does not patch hosts.

mapping_reviews.applicability: IPS signatures or protocol checks can block recognized worm exploit traffic.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Novel exploits, encryption and evasion reduce coverage; false positives can disrupt legitimate service.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Enforcing appropriate SELinux policy restricts resources a container process can access beyond ordinary permissions.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Permissive mode, broad policy and kernel vulnerabilities can undermine confinement.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Namespaces reduce shared resource views as one component of container isolation.
mapping_reviews.limitations: They are not a complete security boundary; host sockets, privileges and kernel defects can permit breakout.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Check changed payment or disclosure instructions through established business evidence and contacts.
mapping_reviews.limitations: A generic instruction to verify must be turned into a defined independent process.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Enforced DMARC reduces certain unauthorized uses of a protected mail domain.
mapping_reviews.limitations: It does not stop fraud through a compromised legitimate mailbox or a look-alike domain and does not validate invoice intent.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Independent financial approvals and payee-change checks constrain the transaction even if email is deceptive.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Collusion, unsafe exceptions and compromised approvers can still undermine the workflow.

mapping_reviews.applicability: Role-specific practice helps executives and assistants recognize authority and confidentiality pretexts.
mapping_reviews.limitations: Senior staff still need enforceable verification procedures and technical controls; training alone is insufficient.

mapping_reviews.applicability: An independently verified request and dual approval can interrupt high-value impersonation before a transfer or disclosure.
